children: Investors no longer need to ask whether corporate America is rolling out artificial intelligence. Second-quarter S&P 500 earnings transcripts show 69% of companies now describe a live deployment, up from 64% a quarter earlier.
The harder question, Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok argues, is who can show that the spending is paying off.

Disclosure collapses once the conversation turns from usage to results. Only 29% of firms attach a number to an outcome. Just 2% report a metric they track over time. None isolate AI as a standalone key performance indicator or a separate line on the profit-and-loss statement.

Where companies do quantify impact, the evidence is lopsided. Cost savings account for about 70% of disclosed proof points; revenue effects make up only 22%. Timing helps explain the imbalance: efficiency gains show up inside existing operations long before new products or sales channels take shape. That still leaves a missing link between AI capital expenditure and the top line.

For markets that have priced in a broad productivity wave, the gap is material. Adoption is no longer the scarce signal. Verifiable return on investment is. Until more companies convert pilots into durable, reportable financial results, Slok’s framing stands: the story has moved from who is deploying AI to who can prove the ROI.

title: From deployment to proof: AI’s ROI test comes into focus
